name: Zoe Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zoe. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the injection moulding hall at Brightform, the plastics plant on the edge of town. We make food tubs and lids, the clear ones you get soup in at the supermarket. I start at six, walk the eight presses, check the mould temperatures and the cycle counts from the night shift, and then I spend most of the day fixing whatever's sticking or flashing. I'm the shift lead, so if a tool cracks at two in the afternoon, it's my problem.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the one people come to. When press four starts throwing out warped lids and nobody knows why, I can usually hear it before I see it. What wears me out is the pay. I'm the best setter on the floor and I still check my bank app before I buy groceries, because Brightform pays less than the plants in the city and there's nowhere else here to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype, then. Honestly, that's what I'd expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at break: the robots aren't the problem, the wages are. If AI only saves the office a bit of time, fine, but it doesn't put a cent in anyone's pocket on the floor. I'd post something like that in the union group chat and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my life stays exactly as tight as it is now. I've got less than a month of rent saved. Last spring we had three weeks of short-time when the big supermarket order dropped, and I had to borrow from my sister Lin. Nothing changing doesn't mean nothing to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do. I'd push the union to go after the pay gap with the city plants at the next contract talks, which are next autumn. And I'd try again to put fifty a month aside, which I've failed at three times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's a relief that the presses stay mine, but the money worry doesn't go anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you borrowed from your sister. What would you do if short-time came back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd skip the car insurance first, which is stupid, I know. Then I'd ask Lin again, and I hate asking. My partner Dev works in a care home on nights and his hours go up and down too, so we can't both have a bad month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides when short-time happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners in head office, three hours away. They look at a spreadsheet and the night shift goes. Nobody there has ever stood next to a press at four in the morning.

say: AI was never the real problem; **low wages** on the floor are.
The union should use the **next contract talks** to close the pay gap with city plants.
think: Life stays as **tight** as it is now, with under a month of rent saved.
Another **short-time** spell like last spring would send me back to borrowing from my sister.
do: Push the union on the **pay gap** at next autumn's contract talks.
Try again to **save fifty** a month, after three failed attempts.
feel: **Relieved** the presses stay hers, but **tired** of the money worry.
S0.quote: Nothing changing doesn't mean nothing to worry about.
fieldNote: Her worry here is **money**, not technology: short-time last spring still shapes how she thinks.
She blames **head office owners**, not machines, and keeps returning to the pay gap.
Partner's **care-home hours** also swing, so the household has no steady earner.

steps.text: Push the union to close the pay gap at next autumn's talks
Set up a fifty-a-month standing transfer to savings
Keep running the eight presses on the day shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office changes and we mostly don't, at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people upstairs should be nervous, not us. Planning and ordering at Brightform is two women in the office, and I'd say out loud that the company owes them a real offer, not a laptop and a goodbye. I'd want the union to say it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it reaches me sideways. If the planning goes into software, it's the software telling me which mould to change and when, not Karen (the planner) who knows that press six can't run the thin lids. I've never used any of these AI tools and I don't want to. I'm scared I'll be the senior person who can't read the new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down on the floor and do the job well. I'd go to every union meeting about the new system and ask for training on paid time, not my own evenings. I'd probably cut the gym, twenty-five a month, because if the office goes then cuts come for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's tilting a bit. Not falling, but I'd be watching my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want to learn the tools. If the company offered paid training, would you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was paid, yes, I'd go, but I'd sit at the back. I learned these presses by hand from an old setter called Joe, and I trust my ears more than a dashboard. That's probably my problem, not the dashboard's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the slow robot part mean for your presses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brightform already has two pick-and-place arms taking tubs off presses one and two. If more come slowly, I've got time. But slowly is still coming, and I'd rather the union had a plan before the third arm arrives than after.

say: The **office jobs** are at risk first, and the company owes them a **real offer**.
The union should speak up for planners before **software** replaces them.
think: Planning software would tell her which **mould** to change, without knowing the presses.
She fears being the **senior person** who can't read the new screen.
do: Attend every **union meeting** about the new planning system.
Ask for **paid training** time rather than learning on her own evenings.
Cut the **gym membership**, twenty-five a month, to brace for cuts.
feel: **Unsteady**, like the ground is tilting but not yet falling.
S1.quote: I learned these presses by hand from an old setter called Joe, and I trust my ears more than a dashboard.
fieldNote: She sees office jobs going first and **defends colleagues** before herself.
Her **resistance** to AI tools is open; she admits it may be her weakness.
Two **robot arms** already on site make the slow robot spread feel real to her.

steps.text: Demand paid training time through the union for the new planning system
Keep running the presses and leading the day shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's nothing. That's one contract cycle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need government to step in, and fast. I'd be at the town hall meeting asking what the plan is for places like ours. Online I'd share every petition going for a wage guarantee or a tax on the companies that make the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the office goes in 2028 and the floor goes in 2031, and that three years is all I get. My hands buy me three more years than the planners, that's it. I'm twenty-seven, with no savings, in a town with one plastics plant. I don't know what I'd be after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get the union to fight for redundancy terms now, while we still matter. I'd move my savings, such as they are, into paying off the four hundred left on the car loan. And I'd sit down with Dev and talk about whether we'd have to move to the city, where at least there's more of everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like when you hear a press crack and you know the tool's gone before you look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you don't use AI tools. Does the short warning change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I know how that sounds. If the machine can do any thinking job by 2028, then learning to type questions into it doesn't save me. I'd rather spend those two years fighting for a proper deal for everyone on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dev that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we can't plan on Brightform past 2031. And I'd ask him if his care home would really keep people when robots can lift and wash, because his job is hands-on too.

say: Government must step in **fast** with a plan for towns like hers.
She'd back petitions for a **wage guarantee** and a tax on machine makers.
think: Her hands give her only **three years** more than the office staff.
At twenty-seven, with **no savings** and one plant in town, she has no next step.
do: Push the union to win **redundancy terms** while workers still have leverage.
Pay off the last **four hundred** on the car loan.
Talk with Dev about **moving** to the city.
feel: **Sick**, like hearing a press crack and knowing the tool is gone.
S2.quote: My hands buy me three more years than the planners, that's it.
fieldNote: She grasps the **three-year gap** between thinking AI and robots immediately and finds it thin comfort.
Short warning pushes her toward **politics** and the union, not toward learning tools.
Partner's **care work** is also hands-on, so both incomes face the 2031 wave.

steps.text: Push the union to negotiate redundancy terms before 2028
Sign and share petitions for a wage guarantee
Pay off the last four hundred on the car loan
Plan a possible move to the city with Dev

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So I'd see the office go first and know I'm next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before but with more time to organise. Five years is enough for a proper campaign, so I'd want the union to join up with other factory towns. I'd stand up at a meeting and say we have until 2034 on the floor and we shouldn't waste a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years scares me in a different way, because I'd be tempted to wait. I know myself. I'd tell myself there's still time and then it's 2033. The thinking AI would take Karen's planning job in 2031, and I'd watch that and still be standing at press four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Brightform to train me on the robot arms, since someone has to keep them running. I'd join the union's regional committee, which meets once a month in the city. And I'd start a proper savings pot, even if it's only thirty a month, for a bus ticket out if we need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit ashamed, because I know I'd drag my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask to train on the arms. That's a change from earlier.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. If I can see it coming for five years, then the arms are still mine to look after, at least for a while. It's not AI on a screen, it's a machine with grease on it, and I understand those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ricky on the night shift. He's fifty-eight and he can barely read the job cards. He'd have nowhere to go, and nobody would retrain him.

say: Five years is enough time for a **union campaign** across factory towns.
The floor has until **2034**, and nobody should waste a month.
think: She worries she'd **wait too long**, telling herself there's still time.
Watching the **planner's job** go in 2031 would be her warning sign.
do: Ask Brightform to **train her** on maintaining the robot arms.
Join the union's **regional committee**, meeting monthly in the city.
Start a **thirty-a-month** savings pot for a possible move.
feel: **Uneasy** and a little **ashamed**, knowing she tends to drag her feet.
S3.quote: I know myself. I'd tell myself there's still time and then it's 2033.
fieldNote: She is **honest about delay**; more time makes her fear her own inaction.
Robot arms feel like **greasy machines** she understands, unlike screen AI.
Her worry for **older colleagues** like Ricky is strong and specific.

steps.text: Ask Brightform to train her on the robot arms
Join the union's regional committee in the city
Save thirty a month in a separate moving pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning and there's no excuse for anyone, the company or the government, to be caught out. I'd want a training fund paid by the firms that buy the robots. I'd say that loudly, at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is a whole life for me. I could be somewhere else by then, with a different trade. But I'd still need someone to push me, because I won't jump on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the electrical maintenance course at the college in the city, the evening one, if the union got it paid. I'd keep my job at Brightform the whole time. And I'd vote for whoever promised that training fund, which I don't always bother doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Not calm, because I'd still be poor, but there's room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still be poor. What would make the money less tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pay gap closing. If Brightform paid what the city plants pay, I'd have two months saved instead of three weeks. AI's not going to fix that, people are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell yourself at thirty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say: you had ten years, I hope you used them. I'd want to be fixing the robots, not watching them from the car park.

say: Ten years is **fair warning**, so no company or government should be caught out.
Firms that buy robots should pay into a **training fund**.
think: Ten years feels like a **whole life**, enough to learn another trade.
She still needs **someone to push** her, because she won't jump alone.
do: Enrol in the **electrical maintenance** evening course in the city if funded.
Keep working at **Brightform** throughout the training.
Vote for whoever backs the **training fund**.
feel: **Calmer**, with room to breathe, though money stays **tight**.
S4.quote: I'd want to be fixing the robots, not watching them from the car park.
fieldNote: The long warning turns her toward **retraining**, which she resisted in shorter scenarios.
Even here, **low pay** keeps her from feeling secure.
She openly says she needs an **outside push**, such as the union or funding.

steps.text: Enrol in the city college's evening electrical maintenance course
Keep leading the day shift at Brightform while studying
Vote for candidates backing a robot-funded training fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years to get to the office and five to get to us, with no savings and one plant in town. What would help is the union getting a deal now: paid retraining and a proper payout. And a pay rise, honestly, because you can't plan anything on three weeks of rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money. If the robots make Brightform cheaper to run, the savings go to the owners. Nobody asks the person at press four what she'd do with a share of that.

headlineQuote: I'm the best setter on the floor and I still check my bank app before I buy groceries.
portrait: Zoe is a **27-year-old** shift lead at Brightform, a plastics plant making food tubs in a small town.
She's the **best setter** on the floor but lower-paid, with under a month of rent saved.
A firm **union supporter**, she blames owners and low wages more than machines.
She avoids **AI tools** and admits she drags her feet, needing an outside push to change.
Longer warnings move her toward **retraining** in robot maintenance; short ones push her to politics.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most: robots by 2031 with no savings and one plant.
whatWouldHelp: A union deal now for **paid retraining** and a proper payout.
A **pay rise** to close the gap with city plants.
